summary: Defines a Transport Model for SNMP that uses TLS or DTLS for authentication and privacy, covering TCP and UDP. It also defines MIB objects to manage the TLS Transport Model. It is a Proposed Standard and was replaced by RFC 6353.

eli5.summary: Wrapping network device messages in a locked envelope so no one can read or change them in transit. It was replaced by RFC 6353.

questions: what ports does snmp over tls use
subtitle: How SNMP messages get certificate-based authentication and encryption by riding inside TLS or DTLS.

tldr.problem: SNMP needs a transport that authenticates both ends and protects management traffic from tampering and eavesdropping, using the certificate infrastructure operators already have.
tldr.mechanism: The TLS Transport Model (TLSTM) sends SNMP messages over TLS on TCP or DTLS on UDP, maps each peer's X.509 certificate to a tmSecurityName, and defines a MIB module for configuring and monitoring it.
tldr.outcome: It was a Standards Track document. It has been obsoleted by RFC 6353 and was updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 5953 was a Proposed Standard. It has been obsoleted by RFC 6353 and was updated by RFC 8996, so see those for the current specification.

sections.title: What the TLS Transport Model Does
sections.content:
RFC 5953 defines a Transport Model for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) that uses either Transport Layer Security (TLS) or Datagram TLS (DTLS). It is called the TLS Transport Model, or TLSTM. It supports SNMP over TLS/TCP and DTLS/UDP. The TLS mode can use TCP's better support for larger packet sizes, and the DTLS mode may work better where a connectionless transport is preferred.

Only X.509 certificate-based authentication is covered. The RFC also defines the SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB, a MIB module for managing the model. It favors SNMP terminology, so it avoids the words manager and agent, and it uses client and server only for the two ends of the (D)TLS connection.
sections.eli5: SNMP is how network gadgets report on themselves. This RFC wraps those reports in a secure tunnel, and the tunnel works over two kinds of delivery: a careful one and a quick one.

sections.title: Where TLSTM Fits and What It Protects Against
sections.content:
The TLSTM is a component of the SNMP Transport Subsystem and sits between the (D)TLS layer and the Message Dispatcher. The sending side hands it unencrypted, unauthenticated messages to pass to (D)TLS, and the receiving side accepts decrypted, integrity-checked messages and passes them up. A session can carry more than one SNMP message, and an implementation MAY close it to save resources.

It addresses the threats named in RFC 3411: modification of information, masquerade, message stream modification, and disclosure. Replay protection uses a Message Authentication Code with a sequence number, and DTLS uses a sliding window. Implementations MUST support authenticating both server and client, and MUST support encryption. Denial of service is not required to be addressed by an SNMP security protocol, but DTLS cookies help against spoofed addresses.

The requested security level (noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv or authPriv) must be met at least, and NULL integrity and encryption algorithms MUST NOT be used to meet authentication or privacy requests.
sections.eli5: It sits between the part that writes messages and the part that sends them, sealing each message on the way out and opening it on the way in. It guards against people changing messages, pretending to be someone else, replaying old ones, or peeking.

sections.title: Certificates and Security Names
sections.content:
Both ends must have X.509 certificates, signed by trusted Certification Authorities or self-signed. Entities SHOULD also have a certificate revocation mechanism, and trusted public keys MUST be installed into the server through a trusted out-of-band mechanism. (D)TLS MUST authenticate both the client and the server.

When a client certificate arrives, the server derives the tmSecurityName using the snmpTlstmCertToTSNTable. Mappings can use a certificate's subjectAltName or CommonName, or a certificate fingerprint tied to a directly specified name. Deployments SHOULD map the subjectAltName. The name must stay constant for a session.

The RFC warns that VACM limits securityNames to 32 octets, so a long name plus a prefix can exceed it. Renegotiation with different certificates MUST NOT be done, so implementations either disable renegotiation (RECOMMENDED) or present the same certificate.
sections.eli5: Each side shows an ID card. The receiver looks the card up on a list to decide what name to call the visitor, and that name cannot change until they leave.

sections.title: Sending, Receiving and Session Handling
sections.content:
For an outgoing message, the model checks that the cached state has the needed values, reuses an existing session for the same domain, address, security name and level, or opens a new one. Errors increment counters such as snmpTlstmSessionOpenErrors. For DTLS over UDP, each SNMP message MUST fit in one UDP datagram, and the server MUST support DTLS cookies, with enabling them by default RECOMMENDED. DTLS replay protection MUST be used.

As a client, it picks a certificate and cipher suites, starts the handshake, and MUST verify the server's certificate is the expected one before sending any SNMP messages. As a server, it MUST request and expect a client certificate and MUST NOT accept SNMP messages until that certificate is authenticated. If anything fails, session establishment MUST fail and a counter is incremented.

Closing a session MUST include sending a close_notify alert. Each session needs a unique tlstmSessionID that does not change during the session.
sections.eli5: Before any message goes through, both sides check each other's ID. If either check fails, the door stays shut and a tally is kept. At the end, each side says goodbye properly.

sections.title: The MIB Module and Assigned Numbers
sections.content:
The SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB defines counters about session usage and errors, configuration tables, and two notifications: snmpTlstmServerCertificateUnknown and snmpTlstmServerInvalidCertificate. Two tables extend the SNMP-TARGET-MIB, naming the client certificate and the expected server identity or fingerprint, and one table maps incoming client certificates to tmSecurityNames. Appendix A gives configuration examples.

IANA assigned default ports for command messages and for notifications, over both TCP and UDP. It also assigned object identifier numbers 8 and 9 under snmpDomains for the two transport domains, 198 under mib-2 for the module, and the prefixes tls and dtls.
sections.eli5: The MIB is a dashboard and settings panel for the secure tunnel. It counts how many sessions opened and failed, and it sounds an alarm if a server shows an unexpected ID.

sections.title: Security and Operational Cautions
sections.content:
(D)TLS only confirms that a certificate was signed by an accepted Certification Authority, so an access control model such as VACM must still authorize requests. Both ends MUST check the certificate presented by the other side against what was expected, to avoid man-in-the-middle attacks. TLSTM clients and servers MUST NOT request, offer or use SSL 2.0, and Perfect Forward Secrecy is RECOMMENDED.

Using SNMPv1, SNMPv2c or USM messages over TLSTM is NOT RECOMMENDED, because they take the security name from the message and not from the authenticated identity. Only SNMPv3 with the Transport Security Model or another secure-transport aware model is recommended. Operationally, implementations SHOULD limit session lifetimes and detect broken sessions, for example with heartbeats.
sections.eli5: A good ID check is not enough by itself. You still need rules about who is allowed to do what, and you should not use old, weak ways of talking through the secure tunnel.
